title: Search-R2: Enhancing Search-Integrated Reasoning via Actor-Refiner Collaboration
one_liner: Search-R2 trains a search agent with a second component that repairs weak reasoning steps and rewards useful retrieval, not just final correctness.
lead: Search-based question answering agents often get only a final right-or-wrong reward. That is a weak training signal because a lucky guess can look good and a mostly correct search path can look bad if the final answer misses. Search-R2 fixes this by splitting the agent into an actor that drafts a reasoning path and a refiner that selectively repairs weak steps, while training with both final-answer reward and a process reward for useful retrieved evidence.

problem.h2: Why sparse reward misguides search-based reasoning
paras: A search-based agent has to decide what to look up, how to combine evidence, and when to revise its current line of thought. If training watches only the final answer, then the system cannot tell which internal search and reasoning choices were helpful.

That creates a credit assignment problem across scales. A long trajectory may contain one useful retrieval and three wasteful ones, but a final correct answer rewards the whole path. A wrong final answer may hide the fact that early evidence gathering was good. Training becomes noisy because the reward does not point to the step that caused success or failure.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Use an actor to draft the trajectory, a refiner to repair weak steps, and a hybrid reward that scores both final correctness and the usefulness of retrieved evidence.

panels.title: 1. The actor searches and drafts an answer path
panels.viz_args: Question -> search -> read evidence -> write intermediate reasoning
panels.caption: The first component generates the initial trajectory.

panels.title: 2. Final reward alone is too coarse
panels.viz_args: Correct final answer can hide wasted search. Wrong answer can hide useful evidence.
panels.caption: The training signal does not identify which steps deserve credit.

panels.title: 3. The refiner inspects weak steps
panels.viz_args: Detect a flawed step, cut there, regenerate the rest.
panels.caption: Selective repair focuses on the parts of the trajectory that likely caused failure.

panels.title: 4. Dense process reward scores retrieved evidence
panels.viz_args: Useful evidence gets reward even before the final answer is known.
panels.caption: The agent now gets guidance about search quality, not only answer outcome.

panels.title: 5. Training favors cleaner search and reasoning
panels.caption: The actor learns better search habits because the refiner and process reward expose where value came from.

steps.text: The actor issues queries, reads retrieved evidence, and writes intermediate reasoning toward an answer.
A second component examines the draft and identifies steps where the search path or reasoning appears faulty.

steps.b: Cut and regenerate from the weak point
steps.text: Instead of rewriting everything, the system cuts the trajectory at the weak step and regenerates the rest from there.
Training uses final correctness plus a step-level reward for whether retrieved evidence is informative for the question.
The actor and refiner improve together because one produces better drafts and the other makes better targeted repairs.

paras: The paper changes both the policy structure and the reward signal. It replaces a single search policy with an actor-refiner pair, and it adds process-level supervision so training can reward useful retrieval even before the final answer is decided.

hidden.name: Step usefulness inside a search trajectory
paras: Step usefulness asks whether a particular retrieval or reasoning step genuinely moved the agent closer to the right answer. This quantity is hidden when training sees only final correctness.

Search-R2 makes usefulness more visible by adding a dense reward for informative evidence and by letting the refiner target weak points. That gives training a clearer signal about which steps should be repeated and which should be changed.

heat.caption: Darker means the step is less useful or more likely to mislead later reasoning.

reads.html: This asks whether a search step actually helped answer the question, because some steps add useful evidence while others only waste queries.
The method estimates step usefulness from evidence density and uses the refiner to repair weak segments, which gives the training process more local credit signals.

paras: The actor-refiner split helps because diagnosis and generation are different jobs. A single component often commits to a bad early step and keeps building on it. The refiner breaks that pattern by examining the trajectory from the outside and rewriting only the weak suffix, so useful early work is preserved while bad later steps are replaced.

The hybrid reward helps because it gives the agent credit for retrieving evidence that actually informs the answer. That reduces reward noise from lucky final answers, and it also preserves signal when the final answer is wrong but some search steps were still good.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Question: Which city hosted the earlier of two events?
The actor first retrieves one relevant article and one irrelevant page.
The final answer is wrong because the later comparison step fails.
Outcome reward is low because the answer is wrong.
Process reward is still partly positive because one retrieved article contained the needed date.
The refiner cuts at the bad comparison step, keeps the useful retrieval, and rewrites the rest.

math.note: The paper formalizes the actor-refiner interaction more fully, but this equation captures the core training idea: final outcome plus process quality.

charts.title: Search-R2

items.html: If the diagnosis step selects the wrong cut point, then regeneration may remove useful work and keep the real mistake because the repair targeted the wrong suffix.
If the step-level reward treats noisy evidence as useful, then the actor may learn to chase flashy but unhelpful retrieval because that behavior is being rewarded.
If the refiner intervenes too often, training and answer-time execution can slow down because many trajectories are being partially regenerated.
The method is strongest on multi-step retrieval tasks, because those are exactly the cases where sparse final reward hides which intermediate steps mattered.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a retrieval question-answering task with multi-hop questions and a small document set. Compare two training setups: one that rewards only final answer correctness and one that adds a refiner plus process reward for useful evidence. Track answer accuracy, number of repeated searches, and whether repaired trajectories reuse good early evidence. The demo should show that the actor-refiner system learns cleaner search behavior because useful steps receive direct credit.
demo.metric_eq: answer_accuracy = correct_answers / total_questions ; search_waste = redundant_queries / total_queries
demo.closing: The demo must show higher answer accuracy with less wasted search.
